name: Archer Push-Up
instructions: Start in a push-up position with hands set very wide, wider than shoulder-width.
Lower your body toward one hand, keeping that arm bent and the other arm straight out to the side.
Push back up to the starting position, then repeat toward the other side.
coachNote: A key progression exercise on the path to a one-arm push-up, shifting nearly all the load onto one arm at a time.
tips: Keep the straight arm as straight as possible throughout.
Keep the hips level, avoiding rotation.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate or sag.
Not shifting enough weight onto the working arm.
benefits: Builds toward a full one-arm push-up.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Build up from a standard wide push-up first.
Keep the wrists in a comfortable position.
startingPosition: Push-up position, hands very wide.
endingPosition: Body lowered toward one bent arm, other arm straight.

name: Pseudo Planche Push-Up
instructions: Start in a push-up position with hands turned so the fingers point toward your feet, positioned near your hips.
Lean your torso forward significantly over your hands as you lower into the push-up.
Push back up to the starting position, maintaining the forward lean throughout.
coachNote: The forward lean shifts significant load onto the shoulders, building foundational planche strength without needing full planche training.
tips: Lean as far forward as your wrist mobility allows.
Keep the core braced to prevent the hips from sagging.
commonMistakes: Not leaning forward enough to get the intended shoulder loading.
Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
benefits: Builds foundational strength for the planche.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Build up wrist mobility and flexibility gradually.
Reduce the forward lean if wrist discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Push-up position, hands near the hips, torso leaned forward.
endingPosition: Body lowered with the forward lean maintained.

name: Spiderman Push-Up
instructions: Start in a standard push-up position.
As you lower down, bring one knee up toward the same-side elbow.
Push back up while returning the leg to the starting position, then repeat bringing the other knee up.
coachNote: Adding the knee drive brings the obliques into play alongside the standard chest and tricep pushing muscles.
tips: Time the knee drive to happen during the descent.
Keep the hips as level as possible.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate excessively.
Rushing through the movement instead of coordinating the timing.
benefits: Adds an oblique and hip mobility component to a standard push-up.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Master a standard push-up first.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Push-up position.
endingPosition: Body lowered, one knee drawn toward the same-side elbow.

name: Hindu Push-Up
instructions: Start in a downward-dog position with hips high and hands and feet on the floor.
Dive your chest forward and down in an arcing motion, ending in an upward-dog-like position with hips low and chest up.
Reverse the arc, pushing the hips back up to return to the starting position.
coachNote: A flowing, dynamic push-up variation from traditional yoga and calisthenics practices that builds mobility alongside pushing strength.
tips: Move through the full arcing range smoothly.
Keep the movement flowing rather than segmented.
commonMistakes: Cutting the range of motion short.
Moving too fast without control.
benefits: Combines pushing strength with shoulder and spine mobility.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Move within a comfortable range of motion for the lower back.
Warm up the shoulders before attempting this.
startingPosition: Downward-dog position, hips high.
endingPosition: Upward-dog-like position, hips low, chest up.

name: Clapping Push-Up
instructions: Start in a standard push-up position.
Lower down, then explosively push up hard enough that your hands leave the floor.
Clap your hands together in the air, then land back in the starting position with soft, bent elbows to absorb the impact.
coachNote: A plyometric push-up variation that develops explosive upper-body power, popular in athletic and combat sports training.
tips: Land softly with bent elbows to absorb the impact.
Build up to this from a regular explosive push-up first.
commonMistakes: Landing with locked elbows, risking injury.
Attempting this before building adequate pushing strength.
benefits: Builds explosive upper-body power.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Practice on a padded or forgiving surface.
Master explosive push-ups without the clap first.
startingPosition: Push-up position.
endingPosition: Landed after clapping in the air.

name: One-Arm Push-Up (Assisted)
instructions: Get into a push-up position with feet spread wide for stability, one hand behind your back or lightly assisting on a low support.
Lower your body down under control using only the working arm.
Push back up to the starting position using the working arm.
coachNote: One of the most impressive calisthenics strength feats — using a light hand-assist or wide foot stance makes this achievable for advanced trainees.
tips: Spread the feet wide for a stable base.
Use a light finger-tip assist from the other hand if needed.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso excessively to compensate.
Attempting this before mastering archer push-ups.
benefits: Extreme unilateral pushing strength builder.
No equipment needed beyond the floor.
safetyNotes: Build up through archer and pseudo planche push-ups first.
Use assistance as needed to maintain good form.
startingPosition: Push-up position, one hand working, feet wide.
endingPosition: Body lowered using only the working arm.

name: Superman Push-Up
instructions: Start in a push-up position, then perform an explosive push-up hard enough to launch your entire body into the air.
While airborne, extend your arms forward and legs back into a flying superman position.
Bring your hands back under your shoulders to land and absorb the impact with bent elbows.
coachNote: An extremely advanced plyometric push-up requiring significant explosive power and landing control — a hallmark calisthenics power move.
tips: Master the clapping push-up before attempting this.
Land softly with bent elbows to absorb the impact.
commonMistakes: Attempting this before building sufficient plyometric pushing power.
Landing with locked elbows or poor hand positioning.
benefits: Extreme explosive upper-body power builder.
Impressive calisthenics skill demonstration.
safetyNotes: Practice on a padded or forgiving surface.
Master easier plyometric push-ups first.
startingPosition: Push-up position.
endingPosition: Landed after extending into a flying position mid-air.

name: Typewriter Push-Up
instructions: Start in a push-up position with hands set very wide.
Lower down toward one hand, then shift your weight side to side at the bottom, sliding across to the other hand while staying low.
Push up from the second side to return to the starting position.
coachNote: Staying low throughout the lateral shift builds significant time-under-tension strength, similar to an archer push-up but with continuous movement.
tips: Keep the chest low throughout the entire side-to-side shift.
Move slowly and with control.
commonMistakes: Rising up during the lateral shift instead of staying low.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Builds significant unilateral pushing strength and control.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Master the archer push-up first.
Keep the wrists in a comfortable position.
startingPosition: Push-up position, hands very wide.
endingPosition: Low position shifted to one side, then the other.

name: Parallel Bar Dip
instructions: Support your body on parallel dip bars with arms extended, torso upright.
Lower your body by bending the elbows until your shoulders are near the level of your elbows.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: A staple calisthenics strength exercise — leaning the torso forward slightly increases chest involvement, while staying upright emphasizes the triceps.
tips: Keep the torso upright for more tricep emphasis.
Control the descent rather than dropping quickly.
commonMistakes: Going too deep and straining the shoulders.
Using momentum by swinging the legs.
benefits: Builds significant tricep and chest strength.
Simple, effective equipment requirement.
safetyNotes: Avoid excessive depth that stresses the shoulder joint.
Build up with assisted dips if needed.
startingPosition: Supported on the bars, arms extended.
endingPosition: Lowered until shoulders are near elbow height.

name: Ring Dip
instructions: Support your body on a pair of gymnastic rings with arms extended, rings turned out slightly.
Lower your body by bending the elbows, keeping the rings close to your body.
Press back up to the starting position while controlling the ring stability.
coachNote: The instability of the rings dramatically increases the shoulder stabilization demand compared to a fixed parallel bar dip.
tips: Turn the rings out slightly at the bottom for shoulder comfort.
Keep the rings close to the body throughout.
commonMistakes: Letting the rings drift away from the body.
Going too deep before building adequate shoulder stability.
benefits: Builds significant shoulder stability alongside tricep strength.
Advanced progression from parallel bar dips.
safetyNotes: Master parallel bar dips before progressing to rings.
Set the rings at an appropriate height with a secure mount.
startingPosition: Supported on the rings, arms extended.
endingPosition: Lowered with control, rings close to the body.

name: Korean Dip
instructions: Position yourself behind parallel bars, gripping them with arms extended, body angled forward.
Lower your body forward and down between or behind the bars, allowing a deep stretch through the chest and shoulders.
Press back up and forward to the starting position.
coachNote: This unique dip variation provides a much deeper chest and shoulder stretch than a standard dip, requiring excellent shoulder mobility.
tips: Move slowly into the stretch, don't force the range.
Keep the core braced throughout.
commonMistakes: Forcing too much range before building adequate shoulder mobility.
Losing control during the deep stretch position.
benefits: Builds tricep and chest strength through an extended range.
Develops shoulder mobility alongside strength.
safetyNotes: Build up range of motion gradually.
Stop if any shoulder discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Behind the bars, arms extended, body angled forward.
endingPosition: Lowered forward and down into a deep stretch.

name: Plyo Push-Up
instructions: Start in a push-up position.
Lower down, then explosively push up hard enough that your hands leave the floor slightly.
Land softly with bent elbows to absorb the impact, then repeat immediately.
coachNote: A great entry point into plyometric pushing before progressing to clapping or superman push-ups.
tips: Focus on exploding up rather than height off the floor.
Land softly with bent elbows.
commonMistakes: Landing with locked elbows.
Not generating enough force to fully leave the floor.
benefits: Builds explosive upper-body power.
Accessible entry point into plyometric push-up training.
safetyNotes: Master a standard push-up before adding the explosive element.
Practice on a forgiving surface.
startingPosition: Push-up position.
endingPosition: Landed softly after leaving the floor.

name: Wall Walk
instructions: Start in a push-up position with your feet against the base of a wall.
Walk your feet up the wall while walking your hands closer to the wall, until your body is nearly vertical.
Walk back down with control to the starting push-up position.
coachNote: One of the best progression exercises for building toward a freestanding handstand, gradually training the shoulders to bear vertical bodyweight.
tips: Move slowly and with control, especially near the top.
Keep the core braced throughout the climb.
commonMistakes: Rushing the climb, losing control near the top.
Arching the lower back excessively at the top.
benefits: Builds toward a freestanding handstand.
No equipment needed beyond a wall.
safetyNotes: Practice near a clear, safe wall space.
Build up the height gradually.
startingPosition: Push-up position, feet at the base of the wall.
endingPosition: Body nearly vertical, hands close to the wall.

name: Ring Push-Up
instructions: Set a pair of gymnastic rings a few inches off the floor and grip one in each hand in a push-up position.
Lower your body down, allowing the rings to turn out naturally.
Press back up to the starting position while controlling the ring stability.
coachNote: The instability of the rings requires significantly more shoulder and core stabilization than a standard floor push-up.
tips: Keep the rings turned out slightly at the bottom for shoulder comfort.
Keep the core braced throughout to control the instability.
commonMistakes: Letting the rings wobble excessively due to a weak core brace.
Rushing the descent without controlling the rings.
benefits: Builds shoulder and core stability alongside pushing strength.
Increases the difficulty of a standard push-up.
safetyNotes: Master a standard push-up first.
Set the rings at a low, stable height to start.
startingPosition: Push-up position, hands gripping the rings.
endingPosition: Body lowered, rings turned out.

name: Muscle-Up (Bar)
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Pull explosively while leaning forward, transitioning your wrists over the bar as your chest reaches bar height.
Press up over the bar to full lockout, finishing in a dip position above the bar.
coachNote: The transition phase, pulling the body over the bar, is the key technical bottleneck that separates this from a simple pull-up.
tips: Use a false grip (wrists over the bar) to make the transition easier.
Pull explosively and lean forward as you approach the bar.
commonMistakes: Pulling straight up like a pull-up instead of leaning forward for the transition.
Attempting this before mastering strict pull-ups and dips.
benefits: A hallmark calisthenics strength and skill movement.
Builds explosive pulling power and transition strength.
safetyNotes: Master strict pull-ups and dips separately first.
Practice the transition with a spotter or resistance band if needed.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, overhand grip.
endingPosition: Locked out above the bar in a dip position.

name: Ring Muscle-Up
instructions: Hang from a pair of gymnastic rings with arms extended.
Pull explosively while leaning forward and turning the rings out, transitioning above them as your chest reaches ring height.
Press up to full lockout, stabilizing the rings in a dip position.
coachNote: Considered more difficult than a bar muscle-up due to the added instability of the rings throughout the entire transition and lockout.
tips: Turn the rings out as you transition for a more stable catch.
Pull explosively and lean forward as you approach the rings.
commonMistakes: Not turning the rings out, leading to an unstable transition.
Attempting this before mastering a bar muscle-up and ring dips.
benefits: Extremely advanced strength and stability skill.
Builds explosive pulling power with maximal shoulder stability demand.
safetyNotes: Master the bar muscle-up and ring dips first.
Set the rings at an appropriate height with a secure mount.
startingPosition: Hanging from the rings, arms extended.
endingPosition: Locked out above the rings in a dip position.

name: Archer Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip.
Pull yourself up toward one hand, keeping that arm bent and the other arm extending straight out to the side.
Lower with control back to the starting position, then repeat toward the other side.
coachNote: A key progression exercise on the path to a one-arm pull-up, shifting nearly all the load onto one arm.
tips: Pull your chin toward the bent-arm hand, not the center.
Keep the straight arm as straight as possible.
commonMistakes: Not shifting enough weight onto the working arm.
Using momentum to swing up instead of a controlled pull.
benefits: Builds toward a full one-arm pull-up.
Significant unilateral back and bicep strength builder.
safetyNotes: Master standard wide-grip pull-ups first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, wide grip.
endingPosition: Pulled up toward one bent arm, other arm extended.

name: L-Sit Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar and raise your legs straight out in front of you to form an L-shape with your body.
While maintaining the L-sit position, pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar.
Lower with control back to the hanging L-sit position.
coachNote: Combining a strict pull-up with an L-sit hold trains the back, biceps, and core simultaneously in one demanding movement.
tips: Keep the legs straight and elevated throughout the entire pull.
Avoid swinging or using momentum.
commonMistakes: Letting the legs drop during the pull.
Using momentum to swing up instead of a controlled pull.
benefits: Combines pulling strength with core and hip flexor endurance.
Advanced progression from a standard pull-up.
safetyNotes: Master both the L-sit hold and strict pull-up separately first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging, legs raised into an L-sit position.
endingPosition: Pulled up with chin over the bar, L-sit maintained.

name: Typewriter Pull-Up
instructions: Pull yourself up to the top of a pull-up with a wide grip, chin over the bar.
While staying at the top, shift your body side to side, sliding from one hand to the other like a typewriter carriage.
Lower down from either side to complete the rep.
coachNote: Staying at the top throughout the lateral shift builds significant time-under-tension strength, similar to an archer pull-up but continuous.
tips: Keep the chin above the bar throughout the entire shift.
Move slowly and with control.
commonMistakes: Dropping below the bar during the shift.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Builds significant unilateral pulling strength and control.
Advanced progression from an archer pull-up.
safetyNotes: Master the archer pull-up first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Top of a pull-up, chin over the bar.
endingPosition: Shifted to one side, then the other, chin still over the bar.

name: Commando Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with a narrow grip, one hand in front of the other, body perpendicular to the bar.
Pull yourself up so your head passes to one side of the bar.
Lower with control, then pull up again so your head passes to the other side.
coachNote: Alternating sides on each rep trains the lats and obliques with a slightly different angle than a standard pull-up.
tips: Keep the pull smooth and controlled on each side.
Alternate sides evenly.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing up instead of a controlled pull.
Only favoring one side.
benefits: Adds an oblique component to standard pulling.
Builds grip and back strength.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Master a standard pull-up first.
startingPosition: Hanging, narrow grip, body perpendicular to the bar.
endingPosition: Pulled up with the head passing to one side of the bar.

name: Scapular Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms fully extended, a passive hang.
Without bending the elbows, pull your shoulder blades down and together, lifting your body slightly.
Return with control to the passive hang position.
coachNote: A foundational drill for building scapular control before progressing to full pull-ups, ensuring the shoulder blades move correctly under load.
tips: Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
Focus on pulling the shoulder blades down and back.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows, turning it into a partial pull-up.
Using momentum instead of a controlled scapular pull.
benefits: Builds foundational scapular control for pull-ups.
Excellent warm-up before pulling exercises.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Keep the movement small and controlled.
startingPosition: Passive hang, arms fully extended.
endingPosition: Shoulder blades pulled down and together, body lifted slightly.

name: Negative Pull-Up
instructions: Use a box or jump to get your chin above a pull-up bar, gripping it with an overhand grip.
Lower yourself down as slowly as possible, resisting the descent the entire way.
Once at the bottom, reset using the box or jump and repeat.
coachNote: One of the best beginner progressions toward a full pull-up, building eccentric strength before concentric strength develops.
tips: Lower as slowly as possible, aiming for several seconds per rep.
Keep the core braced throughout the descent.
commonMistakes: Dropping quickly instead of controlling the full descent.
Swinging during the lowering phase.
benefits: Builds the foundational strength needed for a first full pull-up.
Simple, effective beginner progression.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Use a stable box or platform to reach the top position.
startingPosition: Chin above the bar, arms bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended, hanging.

name: Chest-to-Bar Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull yourself up explosively until your chest, not just your chin, touches the bar.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Requiring significantly more range and power than a standard chin-over-bar pull-up, popular in functional fitness competitions.
tips: Pull the elbows down and back to drive the chest up.
Arch the upper back slightly at the top to make contact.
commonMistakes: Kipping excessively to fake the range instead of pulling strictly.
Not pulling high enough to make chest contact.
benefits: Builds significant back and bicep strength through a large range.
Popular functional fitness benchmark movement.
safetyNotes: Master a standard pull-up first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Pulled up until the chest touches the bar.

name: Towel Pull-Up
instructions: Drape one or two towels over a pull-up bar, gripping the hanging ends firmly.
Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar.
Lower with control back to the starting hanging position.
coachNote: The unstable, thick grip surface significantly increases the forearm and grip demand compared to a standard pull-up.
tips: Grip the towel as firmly as possible throughout.
Keep the pull smooth and controlled.
commonMistakes: Using a grip too weak to complete the set safely.
Letting the towel slip mid-rep.
benefits: Builds exceptional grip and forearm strength alongside back strength.
Simple way to add grip challenge to pull-ups.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar and durable towels.
Master a standard pull-up first.
startingPosition: Hanging from the towels.
endingPosition: Pulled up with chin over the bar.

name: Ring Row
instructions: Set a pair of gymnastic rings to a mid-height, gripping one in each hand while leaning back with feet on the floor and body straight.
Pull your chest up to the rings by driving the elbows back.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Adjustable difficulty by changing the ring height and body angle — steeper angles make it harder, more upright angles make it easier.
tips: Keep the body in a straight line throughout.
Pull the chest to the rings, driving the elbows back.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag during the pull.
Using a body angle too easy or too hard for your current strength.
benefits: Scalable difficulty for all strength levels.
Builds back and bicep strength with adjustable intensity.
safetyNotes: Set the rings at a secure, stable height.
Adjust the body angle to match your strength level.
startingPosition: Leaning back, body straight, arms extended to the rings.
endingPosition: Chest pulled up to the rings.

name: Weighted Pull-Up (Calisthenics)
instructions: Attach a weight plate or weight belt to your body, then hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Once bodyweight pull-ups for high reps become easy, adding external load is the natural progression for continued strength gains.
tips: Use a dip belt for stable, secure weight attachment.
Maintain strict form even with the added load.
commonMistakes: Adding weight before mastering high-rep bodyweight pull-ups.
Using momentum to compensate for the added load.
benefits: Allows continued progressive overload beyond bodyweight.
Builds significant back and bicep strength.
safetyNotes: Use a secure weight attachment method.
Master strict bodyweight pull-ups for high reps first.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar, weight attached.
endingPosition: Pulled up with chin over the bar.

name: Kipping Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Initiate a rhythmic swinging motion with the hips and legs, using the momentum to help drive your chin over the bar.
Push away from the bar at the top to reset for the next rep.
coachNote: A technique-driven pull-up style using body momentum, popular in functional fitness competitions for completing high volumes efficiently.
tips: Generate the kip from the hips, not just the arms.
Time the pull to coincide with the peak of the hip drive.
commonMistakes: Using excessive shoulder strain instead of proper hip timing.
Attempting kipping before mastering strict pull-ups.
benefits: Allows higher-volume pull-up training.
Builds coordination and full-body power.
safetyNotes: Master strict pull-ups before learning to kip.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar with adequate overhead clearance.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Chin over the bar, using kip momentum.

name: Butterfly Pull-Up
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Move your hips in a continuous circular motion, using the momentum to cycle through the pull-up without pausing at the bottom.
Continue the fluid circular rhythm for the desired number of reps.
coachNote: The fastest style of pull-up used in competitive functional fitness, requiring significant practice to master the timing and coordination.
tips: Practice the hip circle pattern without pulling first.
Keep a fast, continuous rhythm once comfortable.
commonMistakes: Attempting this before mastering the kipping pull-up.
Losing the circular rhythm, causing inefficient reps.
benefits: Allows very high-volume pull-up training.
Advanced skill for competitive functional fitness.
safetyNotes: Master the kipping pull-up before progressing to this.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar with plenty of clearance.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Chin over the bar, in continuous circular motion.

name: L-Sit
instructions: Support your body on parallettes or the floor with arms straight, shoulders depressed.
Raise your legs straight out in front of you, forming an L-shape with your torso and legs.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the legs straight and elevated.
coachNote: A foundational calisthenics core and hip flexor strength hold that also serves as a building block for L-sit pull-ups and other advanced skills.
tips: Push down hard through the hands to depress the shoulders.
Keep the legs as straight as possible throughout.
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up instead of depressing them.
Bending the knees to make the hold easier.
benefits: Builds foundational core and hip flexor strength.
Building block for many advanced calisthenics skills.
safetyNotes: Build up hold time gradually.
Use a bent-knee regression if the full L-sit is too difficult.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, legs raised into an L-shape.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: V-Sit Hold
instructions: Support your body on parallettes or the floor with arms straight.
Raise your legs up higher than an L-sit, forming a V-shape between your torso and legs.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the legs straight.
coachNote: A significant progression beyond the L-sit, requiring much greater hip flexor strength and hamstring flexibility to achieve the higher leg angle.
tips: Push down hard through the hands to depress the shoulders.
Work on hamstring flexibility to help achieve the higher angle.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees to compensate for tight hamstrings.
Attempting this before mastering a full L-sit hold.
benefits: Builds advanced core and hip flexor strength.
Impressive calisthenics skill demonstration.
safetyNotes: Master the L-sit before progressing to the V-sit.
Build up hold time and leg height gradually.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, legs raised into a V-shape.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Tuck Planche
instructions: Support your body on parallettes, leaning forward with shoulders past your hands.
Tuck your knees into your chest and lift your feet off the floor, balancing your entire body on your hands.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms straight.
coachNote: The first major progression in the planche series, this teaches the forward lean and full-body balance needed for more advanced planche variations.
tips: Lean forward significantly, shifting the shoulders well past the hands.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Not leaning forward enough to achieve balance.
Bending the elbows to compensate for weak shoulders.
benefits: Foundational strength builder for the planche series.
Builds exceptional shoulder and core strength.
safetyNotes: Build up with pseudo planche push-ups first.
Practice near a soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, leaning forward.
endingPosition: Knees tucked, feet off the floor, balanced on the hands.

name: Advanced Tuck Planche
instructions: Support your body on parallettes, leaning forward with shoulders past your hands.
Tuck your body but extend your hips slightly so your knees are away from your chest, thighs closer to parallel with the floor.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms straight.
coachNote: Extending the hips slightly compared to a basic tuck planche significantly increases the leverage and difficulty of the hold.
tips: Extend the hips gradually as strength improves.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Extending the hips too much before building adequate strength.
Bending the elbows to compensate for weak shoulders.
benefits: Bridges the gap between a tuck planche and a straddle planche.
Builds progressive planche strength.
safetyNotes: Master the basic tuck planche first.
Practice near a soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, leaning forward, hips slightly extended.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Straddle Planche
instructions: Support your body on parallettes, leaning forward with shoulders past your hands.
Extend your legs straight out to the sides in a wide straddle position, fully horizontal to the floor.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms and legs straight.
coachNote: Widening the straddle reduces the leverage demand compared to a full planche, making it a key intermediate step in the progression.
tips: Widen the straddle to reduce the difficulty as needed.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Keeping the legs too narrow before building adequate strength.
Bending the elbows to compensate for weak shoulders.
benefits: Major progression toward a full planche.
Extremely impressive strength and body control demonstration.
safetyNotes: Master the advanced tuck planche first.
Practice near a soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, leaning forward, legs in a wide straddle.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Full Planche
instructions: Support your body on parallettes, leaning forward with shoulders well past your hands.
Extend your legs straight together behind you, fully horizontal to the floor, feet together.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the entire body straight and rigid.
coachNote: One of the pinnacle achievements in calisthenics strength training, requiring years of progressive training through the tuck and straddle stages.
tips: Lean forward as far as needed to find the balance point.
Keep the entire body rigid and straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Attempting this before mastering the straddle planche.
Sagging the hips or bending the knees.
benefits: Represents elite-level calisthenics strength and body control.
Builds extraordinary shoulder, chest, and core strength.
safetyNotes: Only attempt after years of progressive planche training.
Practice near a soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Supported on parallettes, leaning forward, legs together behind.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.

name: Front Lever (Tuck)
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull your body into a horizontal position while tucking your knees into your chest, keeping your back parallel to the floor.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms straight.
coachNote: The first major progression in the front lever series, teaching the horizontal body position and the required lat and core tension.
tips: Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
Pull the shoulder blades down to help stabilize the position.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows to compensate for weak lats.
Letting the hips sag below horizontal.
benefits: Foundational strength builder for the front lever series.
Builds exceptional back and core strength.
safetyNotes: Build up with hollow body holds and pull-ups first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Body horizontal, knees tucked, held statically for time.

name: Front Lever (Advanced Tuck)
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull your body horizontal, extending the hips so your knees move away from your chest, thighs closer to parallel with the floor.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms straight.
coachNote: Extending the hips slightly compared to a basic tuck front lever significantly increases the leverage and difficulty of the hold.
tips: Extend the hips gradually as strength improves.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Extending the hips too much before building adequate strength.
Letting the hips sag below horizontal.
benefits: Bridges the gap between a tuck and straddle front lever.
Builds progressive back and core strength.
safetyNotes: Master the basic tuck front lever first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Body horizontal, hips slightly extended, held statically for time.

name: Front Lever (Straddle)
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull your body horizontal, extending your legs straight out to the sides in a wide straddle.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the arms and legs straight.
coachNote: Widening the straddle reduces the leverage demand compared to a full front lever, making it a key intermediate step in the progression.
tips: Widen the straddle to reduce the difficulty as needed.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Keeping the legs too narrow before building adequate strength.
Letting the hips sag below horizontal.
benefits: Major progression toward a full front lever.
Extremely impressive back and core strength demonstration.
safetyNotes: Master the advanced tuck front lever first.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Body horizontal, legs in a wide straddle, held statically for time.

name: Full Front Lever
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Pull your body fully horizontal, legs straight and together, body forming a straight line from hands to feet.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the entire body rigid and straight.
coachNote: One of the pinnacle back and core strength achievements in calisthenics, requiring years of progressive training through the tuck and straddle stages.
tips: Keep the entire body rigid and straight throughout.
Pull the shoulder blades down to help stabilize the position.
commonMistakes: Attempting this before mastering the straddle front lever.
Letting the hips sag below horizontal.
benefits: Represents elite-level calisthenics back and core strength.
Builds extraordinary total-body tension control.
safetyNotes: Only attempt after years of progressive front lever training.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging from the bar.
endingPosition: Body fully horizontal, held statically for time.

name: Back Lever
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar, then rotate your body through a skin-the-cat motion until you are facing the floor, body horizontal.
Hold the horizontal position with your back facing up, arms straight behind you.
Hold for the desired duration, then rotate back to the starting hanging position.
coachNote: The counterpart to the front lever, training the shoulders and back from the opposite orientation, requiring significant shoulder flexibility.
tips: Keep the body in a straight line throughout the hold.
Build up through a skin-the-cat rotation drill first.
commonMistakes: Sagging the hips or bending at the waist.
Attempting this before building adequate shoulder mobility.
benefits: Builds back and shoulder strength from a unique angle.
Complements front lever training.
safetyNotes: Build up shoulder mobility gradually.
Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
startingPosition: Hanging, rotated to face the floor.
endingPosition: Body horizontal, back facing up, held statically for time.

name: Human Flag
instructions: Grip a vertical pole or bar with one hand high and one hand low, arms straight.
Lift your entire body sideways until it is horizontal to the ground, supported entirely by your arms.
Hold the position for the desired duration, then lower with control.
coachNote: One of the most visually striking calisthenics feats, requiring extreme oblique, shoulder, and lat strength working together to resist gravity sideways.
tips: Build up with a bent-knee tuck flag progression first.
Push down hard with the top arm and pull with the bottom arm.
commonMistakes: Attempting a full flag before building adequate oblique strength.
Letting the hips sag toward the floor.
benefits: Extreme oblique and shoulder strength builder.
Highly impressive calisthenics skill demonstration.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy vertical pole or bar.
Build up through tucked and progressively straighter leg variations.
startingPosition: Gripping the pole, one hand high, one low.
endingPosition: Body horizontal, supported sideways by the arms.

name: Freestanding Handstand
instructions: Place your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart, fingers spread for stability.
Kick up into an inverted position, balancing your entire body weight on your hands.
Hold the handstand, using small finger and wrist adjustments to maintain balance.
coachNote: Balancing without a wall requires far more subtle control than a wall-supported hold — expect a long learning curve using small, controlled falls to practice.
tips: Spread the fingers wide for a stable base.
Make small adjustments with the fingers rather than large corrections.
commonMistakes: Over-correcting balance shifts, causing a fall.
Arching the lower back excessively.
benefits: Builds exceptional shoulder strength and full-body balance.
Foundational skill for many advanced calisthenics moves.
safetyNotes: Practice near a wall or with a spotter while learning.
Learn how to safely bail out of a fall (cartwheel or forward roll).
startingPosition: Standing, hands about to be placed on the floor.
endingPosition: Inverted handstand position, balanced freely.

name: Handstand Walk
instructions: Kick up into a freestanding handstand position.
Shift your weight slightly to one hand and step forward with the other, walking forward on your hands.
Continue for the desired distance, then carefully return to standing.
coachNote: Requires significantly more dynamic balance and shoulder stability than a static handstand hold, popular in functional fitness competitions.
tips: Take small, controlled steps rather than large strides.
Keep the core braced throughout to maintain the straight body line.
commonMistakes: Taking steps too large, causing loss of balance.
Attempting this before mastering a stable static handstand.
benefits: Builds dynamic shoulder strength and balance.
Impressive functional fitness and calisthenics skill.
safetyNotes: Master the freestanding handstand hold first.
Practice in an open, clear space.
startingPosition: Freestanding handstand position.
endingPosition: Walked forward for the set distance while inverted.

name: Elbow Lever (Planche Lever)
instructions: Place your hands on the floor, fingers pointing toward your feet, and rest your hips or thighs on your elbows.
Lean forward and lift your feet off the floor, balancing your entire body horizontally on your hands and elbows.
Hold the position for the desired duration.
coachNote: A more accessible balance and core hold than a full planche, using the elbows as an additional support point.
tips: Position the hips or thighs firmly on the elbows for support.
Lean forward to find the balance point.
commonMistakes: Placing the elbows too far forward or back for stable support.
Rushing to lift the feet before finding balance.
benefits: More accessible entry into planche-style holds.
Builds core and shoulder balance strength.
safetyNotes: Practice near a soft landing surface.
Build up hold time gradually.
startingPosition: Hands on the floor, hips resting on the elbows.
endingPosition: Feet lifted, body balanced horizontally.

name: Tiger Bend Push-Up (Elbow Lever Push-Up)
instructions: Start in an elbow lever position, balanced horizontally with hips resting on the elbows.
Lower your head and chest toward the floor by bending the elbows further.
Press back up to the starting elbow lever position.
coachNote: An advanced dynamic version of the elbow lever, combining a pressing movement with the challenging balance demand of the static hold.
tips: Master the static elbow lever hold before adding movement.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Losing balance during the pressing motion.
Attempting this before mastering the static elbow lever.
benefits: Combines pressing strength with advanced balance control.
Impressive calisthenics skill demonstration.
safetyNotes: Master the static elbow lever first.
Practice near a soft landing surface.
startingPosition: Elbow lever position, balanced horizontally.
endingPosition: Head and chest lowered toward the floor.

name: Freestanding Handstand Push-Up
instructions: Kick up into a freestanding handstand position, balancing without wall support.
Lower your body by bending the elbows until your head nearly touches the floor, maintaining balance throughout.
Press back up to the starting handstand position.
coachNote: One of the most demanding pressing movements in calisthenics — the balance requirement while pressing significant bodyweight overhead is extreme.
tips: Master the freestanding handstand hold before adding the press.
Keep the descent slow and controlled to maintain balance.
commonMistakes: Attempting this before mastering a stable freestanding handstand.
Rushing the press, losing balance.
benefits: Builds extreme shoulder and tricep pressing strength.
Pinnacle calisthenics pressing skill.
safetyNotes: Master wall-supported handstand push-ups first.
Practice near a soft landing surface with a spotter if possible.
startingPosition: Freestanding handstand position.
endingPosition: Lowered until the head nearly touches the floor.

name: Jumping Lunge
instructions: Start in a lunge position, one foot forward and one back, both knees bent.
Jump explosively, switching your leg position in the air.
Land softly in a lunge with the opposite leg forward, then immediately repeat.
coachNote: A dynamic plyometric progression from static lunges, building explosive power and coordination in a split-stance position.
tips: Land softly with bent knees to absorb the impact.
Keep the torso upright throughout each jump.
commonMistakes: Landing with stiff, locked knees.
Losing balance on the landing due to poor control.
benefits: Builds explosive unilateral leg power.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Master static lunges before adding the jump.
Practice on a surface with adequate cushioning.
startingPosition: Lunge position, one foot forward.
endingPosition: Landed in a lunge with legs switched.

name: Broad Jump
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, swinging your arms back as you dip into a quarter squat.
Explosively jump forward as far as possible, swinging the arms forward to help drive distance.
Land softly with bent knees, absorbing the impact fully before resetting.
coachNote: A classic horizontal power test used widely in athletic testing and training, measuring explosive leg power in the forward direction.
tips: Use a full arm swing to help generate momentum.
Land softly and stick the landing before resetting.
commonMistakes: Landing stiff-legged, increasing injury risk.
Not using the arms to help generate forward power.
benefits: Builds explosive horizontal power.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Land on a surface with adequate cushioning.
Ensure enough clear space to land safely.
startingPosition: Standing, quarter squat, arms back.
endingPosition: Landed forward with both feet, knees bent.

name: Depth Jump
instructions: Stand on top of a box, then step off (don't jump) and land on the floor with both feet.
The instant your feet touch the ground, explode immediately into a maximal vertical jump.
Land softly after the jump to complete the rep.
coachNote: This trains reactive strength — the ability to rapidly switch from absorbing force to producing force, a key quality in explosive sports.
tips: Minimize the ground contact time between landing and jumping.
Use a box height appropriate to your strength and landing ability.
commonMistakes: Using a box too high, causing dangerous landing forces.
Pausing too long on the ground instead of reacting immediately.
benefits: Builds reactive strength and explosive power.
Highly effective for improving jump and sprint performance.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate box height, typically 12-24 inches to start.
Only perform this once other jump training is well established.
startingPosition: Standing on the box.
endingPosition: Landed after the reactive vertical jump.

name: Single-Leg Box Jump
instructions: Stand on one leg facing a plyometric box, other leg lifted.
Bend the standing knee slightly, then explosively jump up onto the box using only that leg.
Land softly on the box with the same leg, then step down and repeat before switching sides.
coachNote: Training explosive jumping on a single leg builds significant unilateral power that transfers directly to sprinting and cutting sports.
tips: Use a lower box height than your bilateral box jump.
Land fully stable on the box before standing tall.
commonMistakes: Using a box too high before building adequate single-leg power.
Landing with poor knee alignment.
benefits: Builds significant unilateral explosive power.
Highly transferable to sprinting and cutting sports.
safetyNotes: Master a bilateral box jump before attempting this.
Use a much lower box height than your bilateral capacity.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg facing the box.
endingPosition: Landed on the box on the same leg.

name: Frog Jump
instructions: Start in a deep squat position with your hands touching the floor between your feet.
Explosively jump forward, driving through the legs and swinging the arms for momentum.
Land softly back in the deep squat position and immediately repeat.
coachNote: A demanding plyometric exercise combining deep squat mobility with explosive forward power, popular in athletic conditioning circuits.
tips: Land softly back into the full squat position.
Keep the movement continuous rather than pausing between jumps.
commonMistakes: Not landing in a full squat, reducing the training effect.
Landing with stiff, locked knees.
benefits: Builds explosive power and lower-body endurance together.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Land on a surface with adequate cushioning.
Build up from bodyweight squats before adding the jump.
startingPosition: Deep squat, hands on the floor.
endingPosition: Landed forward in the deep squat position.

name: Duck Walk
instructions: Get into a deep squat position with your hands on your hips or in front for balance.
Walk forward while staying in the deep squat position, taking small steps.
Continue for the desired distance.
coachNote: A simple, effective way to build hip and ankle mobility while placing continuous tension on the quads in a deep squat position.
tips: Keep the squat as deep as your mobility allows.
Take small, controlled steps.
commonMistakes: Rising up out of the deep squat position while walking.
Taking steps too large, causing loss of balance.
benefits: Builds hip and ankle mobility.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Move within a comfortable range of motion.
Build up the distance gradually.
startingPosition: Deep squat position.
endingPosition: Walked forward while remaining in the deep squat.

name: Lateral Bound (Skater Jump)
instructions: Stand on one leg, then bend the knee slightly and jump laterally to the side.
Land softly on the opposite leg, absorbing the impact while maintaining balance.
Immediately jump back in the other direction, continuing to alternate sides.
coachNote: This trains lateral power and single-leg stability, both highly transferable to field and court sports requiring quick direction changes.
tips: Land softly with a bent knee to absorb the impact.
Hold the landing briefly to demonstrate control before jumping back.
commonMistakes: Landing with poor knee alignment, caving inward.
Rushing between jumps without controlling the landing.
benefits: Builds lateral power and single-leg stability.
Highly transferable to sports requiring quick direction changes.
safetyNotes: Land on a surface with adequate cushioning.
Build up from smaller jumps before increasing distance.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg.
endingPosition: Landed laterally on the opposite leg.

name: Tuck Jump
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Jump explosively upward, driving both knees up toward your chest at the peak of the jump.
Land softly with bent knees, absorbing the impact before immediately repeating.
coachNote: A demanding vertical plyometric exercise that requires both power and core strength to drive the knees high enough for a full tuck.
tips: Drive the knees as high as possible at the peak of the jump.
Land softly with bent knees to absorb the impact.
commonMistakes: Not driving the knees high enough to achieve a real tuck.
Landing with stiff, locked knees.
benefits: Builds explosive vertical power and core strength.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Land on a surface with adequate cushioning.
Build up from a standard vertical jump first.
startingPosition: Standing, feet shoulder-width apart.
endingPosition: Landed after tucking the knees at the peak of the jump.

name: Muscle-Up Negative
instructions: Start in the top position of a muscle-up, supported above the bar with arms extended.
Slowly lower your body back through the transition, controlling the descent through the dip and pull-up phases.
Finish in a full hang once the descent is complete, resetting to the top by any means for the next rep.
coachNote: One of the best training tools for building the strength and confidence needed for the tricky muscle-up transition phase.
tips: Lower as slowly as possible through the entire transition.
Focus especially on controlling the hardest part, around chest height at the bar.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the transition instead of controlling it.
Skipping straight to full muscle-up attempts without this progression.
benefits: Builds the specific strength needed for the muscle-up transition.
Effective progression exercise for an advanced skill.
safetyNotes: Use a secure, sturdy pull-up bar.
Get to the top position with a jump or box assist if needed.
startingPosition: Top of a muscle-up, supported above the bar.
endingPosition: Lowered through the transition to a full hang.

name: Handstand Push-Up Negative
instructions: Kick up into a handstand against a wall for support.
Lower your body as slowly as possible by bending the elbows until your head lightly touches the floor.
Come out of the position with control, then reset and repeat.
coachNote: A key building block for a full handstand push-up, developing the eccentric strength needed before the concentric press is achievable.
tips: Lower as slowly as possible, aiming for several seconds per rep.
Use a wall for support and stability.
commonMistakes: Dropping quickly instead of controlling the full descent.
Attempting this before mastering a solid handstand hold.
benefits: Builds the eccentric strength needed for a full handstand push-up.
Effective beginner-to-intermediate progression.
safetyNotes: Use a soft surface for the head to touch down on.
Practice against a sturdy wall.
startingPosition: Handstand against the wall.
endingPosition: Lowered until the head lightly touches the floor.

name: Assisted Pistol Squat (Wall/TRX)
instructions: Stand on one leg holding a suspension strap, doorframe, or sturdy support for light assistance.
Extend the other leg forward and squat down on the standing leg as low as possible, using the support to maintain balance.
Drive through the standing leg to return to standing.
coachNote: This removes the balance component of a full pistol squat, letting beginners focus on building the necessary single-leg strength and ankle mobility first.
tips: Use only as much assistance as needed from the support.
Keep the extended leg as straight as possible.
commonMistakes: Relying too heavily on the support instead of the working leg.
Rushing to remove the assistance before building adequate strength.
benefits: Accessible progression toward a full pistol squat.
Builds single-leg strength and ankle mobility.
safetyNotes: Use a stable, secure support.
Progress by gradually reducing the amount of assistance.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg, holding a support.
endingPosition: Squatted low on the standing leg, assisted by the support.

name: Pike Walk
instructions: Start in a pike position with hips high, hands and feet on the floor, legs relatively straight.
Walk your hands forward while keeping the hips elevated and legs straight, walking the feet to follow.
Continue the walking pattern for the desired distance.
coachNote: A useful bridge exercise between a downward-dog stretch and full handstand training, loading the shoulders while keeping ground contact.
tips: Keep the hips high and legs as straight as possible throughout.
Take controlled, deliberate steps with the hands.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drop, turning it into a bear crawl.
Bending the knees excessively to compensate for tight hamstrings.
benefits: Builds shoulder strength and hamstring flexibility together.
Bridges toward more advanced handstand training.
safetyNotes: Move within a comfortable range of motion.
Keep the wrists in a comfortable position.
startingPosition: Pike position, hips high.
endingPosition: Walked forward while maintaining the pike position.

name: Planche Lean
instructions: Get into a push-up or plank position with your hands under your shoulders.
Lean your torso and shoulders forward past your hands as far as comfortable, keeping the arms straight.
Hold the leaned position for the desired duration, then return to the starting position.
coachNote: The very first step in the entire planche progression, building the wrist and shoulder tolerance for the extreme forward lean required.
tips: Increase the lean gradually as wrist and shoulder tolerance improves.
Keep the arms completely straight throughout.
commonMistakes: Leaning too far too soon before building adequate wrist tolerance.
Bending the elbows to compensate.
benefits: Builds foundational wrist and shoulder tolerance for planche training.
Simple, beginner-friendly starting point.
safetyNotes: Build up the lean angle and hold duration gradually.
Stop if any wrist pain occurs.
startingPosition: Plank position, hands under the shoulders.
endingPosition: Torso leaned forward past the hands.

name: Wall-Assisted Handstand Hold
instructions: Place your hands on the floor a short distance from a wall, fingers spread.
Kick up into a handstand, resting your heels lightly against the wall for balance support.
Hold the position for the desired duration, keeping the body as straight as possible.
coachNote: The essential first step for anyone learning a handstand, building the necessary shoulder strength and inverted body awareness safely.
tips: Keep the body in as straight a line as possible.
Rely on the wall lightly, not as a full crutch.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back excessively, creating a banana shape.
Relying too heavily on the wall instead of engaging the shoulders and core.
benefits: Beginner-friendly introduction to inverted holds.
Builds foundational shoulder and core strength.
safetyNotes: Practice near a sturdy, clear wall.
Learn how to safely exit the position by cartwheeling out or stepping down.
startingPosition: Hands on the floor near the wall.
endingPosition: Handstand position, heels resting against the wall.

name: Ring Support Hold
instructions: Support your body on a pair of gymnastic rings with arms fully extended, rings turned out slightly.
Hold the position steady, keeping the rings as still as possible and the body straight.
Hold for the desired duration, then dismount with control.
coachNote: A foundational strength and stability hold for all ring-based calisthenics training, teaching shoulder depression and ring control before dipping.
tips: Depress the shoulders down away from the ears.
Turn the rings out slightly for a more stable, comfortable position.
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears.
Letting the rings wobble excessively due to a weak core brace.
benefits: Builds foundational shoulder stability for ring training.
Prerequisite skill for ring dips and muscle-ups.
safetyNotes: Set the rings at a secure, stable height.
Build up hold duration gradually.
startingPosition: Supported on the rings, arms extended.
endingPosition: Same position, held statically for time.
